title: International Financial Management
outcomes: Evaluate foreign projects from the parent's perspective.
Explain IFCs, GIFT City and sovereign funds.

meta.exam_tip: Discount foreign flows at a foreign rate or home flows at a home rate — never mix.

concepts.title: International capital budgeting
body: Foreign projects are more complex: cash flows differ between the project and the parent (remittance restrictions, taxes, transfer prices, royalties and fees), exchange rates fluctuate, inflation rates differ, political and country risks exist, and subsidised financing may be available.

Approaches: (1) discount foreign currency flows at a foreign-currency rate, then convert the NPV at spot; or (2) convert flows at forecast exchange rates (via PPP or IRP) and discount at the home rate — the results agree if parity holds. The parent's perspective (remittable cash flows) decides the investment.

Adjusted present value suits foreign projects: base NPV plus PV of financing side effects such as subsidised loans and tax shields. Scenarios include a foreign firm investing in India, and an Indian firm investing abroad with funds raised in the same or a different country.
concepts.analogy: Value what the parent can actually bring home.
concepts.work: A project with blocked profits is worth less to the parent than to the subsidiary.

concepts.title: International sources of finance
body: Foreign currency convertible bonds (FCCBs) are bonds issued abroad in foreign currency, convertible into equity of the issuer; low coupons but currency and redemption risk if not converted.

Depository receipts: ADRs are issued in the US and traded on US exchanges; GDRs are issued in multiple markets, often listed in Luxembourg or London. A depository bank abroad issues receipts against shares held by a custodian in India.

Other sources: external commercial borrowings, euro-convertible bonds, euro bonds and foreign bonds (e.g. Yankee, Samurai, masala bonds — rupee-denominated bonds issued abroad), syndicated loans and export credit.
concepts.analogy: Global markets offer cheaper or larger funds — with currency and regulatory strings.
concepts.work: A masala bond lets an Indian company borrow abroad without taking currency risk.

concepts.title: International financial centres, GIFT City and sovereign funds
body: An international financial centre (IFC) serves non-residents and residents in foreign currency transactions — banking, capital markets, insurance, asset management — with competitive regulation and tax.

GIFT City in Gujarat houses India's International Financial Services Centre, regulated by the IFSCA, offering tax benefits, international exchanges, banking units and fund management, aiming to bring offshore financial business onshore.

Sovereign wealth funds are state-owned investment funds (from commodity revenues, trade surpluses or reserves) that invest globally in equities, bonds, infrastructure and private assets; they provide long-term capital but raise governance and strategic concerns.
concepts.analogy: IFCs and sovereign funds shape global capital flows.
concepts.work: An Indian firm can list bonds on an exchange in GIFT IFSC.

concepts.title: International working capital management
body: Multinational cash management aims to minimise idle cash, currency and tax costs: accelerating inflows, managing blocked funds (via royalties, fees, transfer pricing, parallel loans), leading and lagging, netting of intra-group payments, and centralised investment of surplus cash.
Transfer pricing can shift profits to lower-tax jurisdictions, but is constrained by arm's-length rules and tax authorities.
International inventory management weighs stockpiling against currency changes and supply disruptions; receivables management covers credit terms, currency of invoicing, factoring and forfaiting.
concepts.analogy: Centralise, net and time payments to save cost.
concepts.work: Netting cut three payments totalling 120 to two payments totalling 20.

illustrations.title: Evaluating a US project
illustrations.q: An Indian company considers a US project costing USD 1,000 thousand now, generating USD 400, 500 and 600 thousand in years 1–3. The USD required return is 10%. Spot is ₹84/USD; Indian inflation 6% and US inflation 2%. Compute the NPV in USD and in rupees (home-currency equivalent at spot), and the expected year-1 spot rate.

mcqs.explain: Only cash reaching the parent creates value for its shareholders. In practice: consider restrictions.

mcqs.q: GIFT City IFSC is regulated by:

summary: Two consistent NPV approaches; APV for subsidies.
FCCB, ADR, GDR, ECB, masala bonds.
remember: Blocked funds reduce value to parent.

viva.q: Why may project and parent cash flows differ?
viva.model: Because of remittance restrictions, taxes, transfer pricing, royalties and fees, and exchange rate effects.
ADRs are issued and traded in the US; GDRs are issued in several markets and usually listed in Europe.
India's international financial services centre in Gujarat, regulated by IFSCA, for offshore financial business.
Offsetting intra-group receivables and payables so that only net amounts are transferred.

viva.q: How can APV help foreign projects?
viva.model: It values the base project separately and adds financing benefits such as subsidised loans and tax shields.

cases.title: Indus Pharma Global
cases.case: Indus Pharma's German subsidiary can remit only 50% of profits each year; the rest is blocked. Profits are EUR 10 million a year. Spot is ₹90/EUR. Indus is considering a GDR issue in Luxembourg and an FCCB with a 1% coupon.

mcqs.explain: 50% of 10. In practice: parent cash flow.

mcqs.q: Rupee value of remittance at spot (₹ crore):
mcqs.explain: 5 million × 90 = ₹45 crore. In practice: forecast future rates.
Receipts represent shares. In practice: listed abroad.

mcqs.q: A key risk of the FCCB is:
options: Repaying principal in foreign currency if not converted
mcqs.explain: Currency and redemption risk. In practice: falling share prices deter conversion.
